## Setting up the problem

"Cost‑competitive with lithium‑ion" only makes sense if both systems are delivering the same thing. Li‑ion batteries store and return **electricity**. A molten‑salt tank only stores **heat** — to compare it to a battery you need to add a charging path (electric heater) and a discharging path (heat engine, e.g. a small steam turbine or ORC) that convert back to electricity. That round‑trip conversion is where thermal storage usually wins or loses, so I'll build the estimate on that electricity‑in/electricity‑out basis, and flag the heat‑only case separately since it's a very different (and much more favorable) comparison.

## 1. Storage medium (the salt itself)

Solar salt (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃), operated between ~290°C and ~565°C:
- ΔT ≈ 275 K, cp ≈ 1.5 kJ/kg·K → specific energy ≈ 0.115 kWh_th/kg
- 5 MWh = 5,000 kWh_th → mass needed ≈ 5,000 / 0.115 ≈ **43.6 tonnes**
- Salt cost ≈ $700/tonne → **≈ $30,000**

That's only **~$6/kWh_th** — this is the part of the system that scales beautifully and is genuinely cheap. It is *not* where the cost problem lives.

## 2. Tanks, insulation, foundations

Salt density ≈ 1,800 kg/m³ → volume ≈ 24 m³; with freeboard, two tanks (hot + cold) each ~29 m³. At small, custom-fabricated scale (refractory lining for the 565°C tank, trace heating, nitrogen blanketing to stop oxidation), insulated vessel fabrication runs ~$1,000–1,500/m² of surface area:
- Each tank ≈ 56 m² surface → ≈ $85,000/tank × 2 ≈ $170,000
- + foundations/heat-traced piping interfaces (+30%) ≈ **$220,000**

## 3. Pumps, piping, valves, N₂ blanket, controls

Molten salt freezes above 200°C and is corrosive, so everything needs trace heating and special alloys/seals:
- Salt pumps (hot + cold side): ~$100,000
- Piping, valves, trace heat, N₂ system: ~$80,000
- Instrumentation/controls: ~$50,000
- **Subtotal ≈ $230,000**

## 4. Charging (electric resistance heater)

Charge over ~4 h → ~1.25 MW heater, at ~$100/kW industrial immersion heater: **≈ $125,000**

## 5. Discharging — the dominant term

If the output is electricity, you need a small steam generator + turbine (or ORC). Small power blocks (<2 MWe) have no economy of scale — **$2,000–3,000/kW installed** is typical. At ~1.25 MW output: **≈ $3,100,000**.

This single line item is 3–4x everything else combined.

## Rolling it up

| Component | Cost |
|---|---|
| Salt | $30,000 |
| Tanks + foundations | $220,000 |
| Pumps/piping/BOP | $230,000 |
| Electric heater (charge) | $125,000 |
| Turbine/ORC (discharge) | $3,100,000 |
| Subtotal | $3,705,000 |
| +30% EPC/engineering/contingency | $1,110,000 |
| **Total installed** | **≈ $4.8M** |

**≈ $970/kWh of storage capacity** — roughly 3–5x a current utility-scale Li-ion system ($150–250/kWh installed).

## Amortized over cycle life

Molten salt tanks have no electrochemical degradation — mechanical life ~20–25 years, say 1 cycle/day → ~7,300 cycles. Round-trip efficiency (heater ~98% → storage losses ~95% → small low-temp turbine ~40%) ≈ **~40% electric-to-electric**.

Energy delivered over life = 5 MWh × 0.40 × 7,300 ≈ 14,600 MWh
**Capital cost per kWh delivered ≈ $4.8M / 14.6M kWh ≈ $0.33/kWh**

Li-ion LFP (≈$200/kWh installed, ~90% RTE, ~5,000 cycles):
Energy delivered = 5 MWh × 0.90 × 5,000 ≈ 22,500 MWh
**≈ $1M / 22.5M kWh ≈ $0.044/kWh**

## Verdict: not competitive at this scale — for electricity

At 5 MWh, molten-salt thermal storage is **~7–8x more expensive per kWh delivered** than lithium-ion, when the job is storing and returning *electricity*. The problem isn't the salt (it's dirt cheap) — it's that a small power-conversion block has terrible $/kW economics and the round-trip efficiency through a heat engine (~40%) is much worse than a battery's (~90%).

This flips if the end-use is **heat, not electricity** (no turbine needed — e.g. an industrial process-heat "thermal battery," which is what real products like Rondo Energy are actually selling). Drop the $3.1M power block, keep everything else: installed cost falls to ≈$865k (**≈$173/kWh_th**), RTE rises to ~95% (just resistive-heat-to-storage-to-heat losses), and cycle life is effectively unlimited (not generator-bound). That works out to roughly **$0.02/kWh delivered** — about **2x cheaper** than using a battery plus a resistive heater to do the same job.

**Bottom line:** the salt and tank are cheap at any scale; the economics live entirely in what you attach to them. For electricity-to-electricity storage at 5 MWh, molten salt loses badly to Li-ion because small power blocks are expensive and thermal round-trip efficiency is low — you'd need to scale into the 100s of MWh range (CSP-plant territory) before the power block and tanks get cheap enough per kWh to compete. For electricity-to-heat storage, molten salt is already cheaper than batteries today, which is exactly the niche it's being commercialized into.
